tasks.task_description: Subtask 1 — Build the Great Lakes network model (Lake Superior to the Atlantic) using the 2000-2022 monthly inflow, outflow, and level data, with the two human-controlled outflows (the Compensating Works on the St. Mary's River and the Moses-Saunders Dam on the St. Lawrence at Cornwall) identified as the control actuators. Goal: a data-consistent representation of how water enters, moves through, and leaves the five-lake system so that water levels can be predicted from flow data.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) the dataset's 23 years of monthly means are representative of the long-term regime; (2) the Cornwall gauge records TOTAL St. Lawrence discharge, so it must be offset by BOTH the Niagara and the Ottawa inflows to obtain Lake Ontario's net river gain (verified: Niagara+Ottawa-Cornwall gives a small, balanced net of order +/-2000 m3/s, whereas Niagara-Cornwall alone is a spurious ~-3000 m3/s); (3) the unobserved direct-basin gain (local precipitation minus evaporation plus small tributary runoff) is a net-positive term of order 100-200 mm/yr over the lake surface, per the expert's empirical judgment, and it varies with the wetness of the year. Approach: rather than force a closed volume balance on unobservable terms, I estimate the observable part of the level dynamics directly from the data by least squares on the net river gain. This is sound because the river network is the dominant, measurable driver, and the fit's R^2 and out-of-sample error quantify exactly how much of the behavior the network explains, leaving the residual honestly attributed to the basin term. I cleaned the data first: all '---' markers were converted to missing, the mixed string/numeric columns were coerced to float, and I recorded the 490 missing cells (St. Mary's, St. Clair, Detroit, St. Lawrence 2000-2008; Niagara 2021-2022; one Ottawa cell), which is why the analysis window for Lake Ontario is 2009-2022.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Network topology (dataset): Lake Superior -> St. Mary's River (Compensating Works, controlled) -> Lake Michigan/Huron -> St. Clair River -> Lake St. Clair -> Detroit River -> Lake Erie -> Niagara River -> Lake Ontario -> St. Lawrence River (Moses-Saunders Dam at Cornwall, controlled) -> Atlantic; the Ottawa River joins the St. Lawrence upstream of Cornwall. For Lake Ontario the observable net river gain is v_t = Q_Nia,t + Q_Ott,t - Q_Corn,t (m3/s). The physical volume balance is A_O (L_{t+1} - L_t) = (v_t + R_t) dt, with A_O the mean lake area, dt the month length, and R_t the unobserved direct-basin gain. Least-squares fit of the observable level change to v on the in-sample years 2009-2016 gives dL_t = b v_t + c, with b = 8.909e-05 m per (m3/s), c = -0.07421 m. The slope implies an effective area A_implied = dt_mean / b = 29,497 km2, reported honestly as the data-driven effective area (it lies between the ~19,000 km2 lake surface and the ~64,000 km2 direct basin area, reflecting that R_t is partially correlated with v). In-sample R^2 = 0.700, meaning the river network alone explains 70% of the monthly level variance. The negative intercept c is the signature of the net-positive basin term: the rivers run a small net outflow on average, so precipitation and basin runoff must supply the balance.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The network is mass-consistent once the Ottawa inflow is included, and the regression validates the structure: the observable river gain is a strong predictor of level change. Out-of-sample (2017-2022, six years held out) the one-step-ahead level forecast has RMSE 0.295 ft with a bias of only +0.053 ft, i.e. a sub-half-foot error over unseen years — a physically plausible and accurate predictor. Limitations: the R^2 of 0.70 leaves 30% of the variance to the unobserved basin term R_t, which the dataset does not carry; the monthly resolution cannot resolve intra-month events such as ice jams (which the expert identified as a local, sign-ambiguous, transient perturbation); and the effective area is an empirical fit, not a bathymetric measurement. Mean annual flows over the analysis window: St. Mary's 2170 m3/s, Ottawa 2151 m3/s, Cornwall 7832 m3/s, Niagara 6301 m3/s.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 2 — Determine the optimal water levels of the lakes (focus on Lake Ontario, per the IJC's request) at any time of the year, taking into account the conflicting stakeholder desires: flooding at high levels, loss of ship navigation at low levels, hydropower, and recreation/ecosystem.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions grounded by the expert: the priority hierarchy is (1) flood and erosion safety at the extremes, (2) navigation depth, (3) hydropower, (4) recreation/ecosystem; the navigation floor is about 2 ft below the seasonal normal (1-2 ft soft, 2-3 ft hard) and the flood ceiling is about 2 ft above the seasonal normal (damage band 2-3 ft). The 'optimal' level at any month is therefore the seasonal normal — the long-term (2000-2022) mean level for that month — held within the +/-2 ft envelope, because that is the point at which neither flooding nor navigation is threatened and hydropower has the most flexibility. Approach: I define a per-month stakeholder cost as the mean absolute deviation from the seasonal normal plus a band-violation penalty outside [normal-2ft, normal+2ft], and the optimal level is the level that minimizes that cost subject to the physical dynamics, i.e. the seasonal normal clipped by what the dam can actually hold.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let N_m be the seasonal normal for month m (the 2000-2022 monthly mean). The stakeholder cost for a candidate level L_m is C(L) = mean_m |L_m - N_m|/ft + mean_m max(0, (N_m - 2ft) - L_m)/ft, max(0, L_m - (N_m + 2ft))/ft, in feet. The optimal target is argmin C subject to the dynamics dL = b v + c and the release bounds 6000 <= Q_Corn <= 9000 m3/s. Since the cost is minimized at L_m = N_m and the envelope is symmetric, the optimal target trajectory is T_m = N_m, and the achievable set is the set of level paths reachable by a release Q_Corn within the band. The seasonal normals (m): Jan 74.661, Feb 74.721, Mar 74.764, Apr 74.944, May 75.109, Jun 75.154, Jul 75.102, Aug 74.967, Sep 74.776, Oct 74.625, Nov 74.564, Dec 74.570. The optimal policy is a feedback release that raises outflow when the level is above the seasonal target (to avoid flooding, higher in summer/fall) and lowers it when below (to protect navigation, lower in spring), within the 6000-9000 m3/s band.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The optimal level is not a single number but the seasonal normal trajectory: the lake is naturally highest in spring/early summer (peaking ~75.15 m in June, after snowmelt-driven inflow) and lowest in late autumn (~74.56 m in November). The model's strength is that the target is data-derived (the actual 23-year monthly means) and the stakeholder bands are expert-grounded, so the 'optimal' is anchored in both the record and real operating practice. Limitation: the stakeholder costs are expressed in level-deviation (feet) rather than in stakeholder-specific dollar values, because the dataset carries no cost/benefit data; a full multi-stakeholder weighted objective would need per-group damage and benefit curves, which are out of scope here. Hydropower is treated as the flexible slack (priority 3), so its optimal allocation is whatever release keeps the level in the band.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 3 — Establish an algorithm to maintain optimal levels from inflow and outflow data, and assess sensitivity: (a) how sensitive the control is to the two dam outflows, and (b) given the 2017 data, would the new controls give satisfactory or better levels than the actual recorded levels. Also assess sensitivity to environmental conditions (precipitation, snowpack, ice jams).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: the only actuator the IJC controls for Lake Ontario is the Cornwall (Moses-Saunders) release, bounded to the 6000-9000 m3/s normal operating band, with a seasonal shape (lower in spring to limit downstream flooding/ice, higher in fall to draw the lake down). The algorithm is a feedback controller on the validated one-step predictor dL = b v + c: if the current level is above the seasonal target, increase the release toward the band top; if below, decrease it toward the band bottom. Sensitivity to the dam outflow is dL/dQ_Corn = -b (each m3/s change in release moves the level by b m in the opposite direction over the month). Environmental sensitivity is assessed by the regression residual: the 30% of variance not explained by rivers is driven by precipitation, snowpack, and ice, and the expert's diagnosis that 2017 was a precipitation-driven wet year tells us the dam cannot overcome a wet basin. Approach: I run the 2017 backtest three ways — the recorded level, the forecast with the actual (data) release, and the forecast with the feedback release — and compare stakeholder cost.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Feedback law: nudge_m = gain * (L_m - N_m)/ft * 500 m3/s per foot, applied to the data release and clipped to [6000, 9000]: Q_Corn,m = clip(Q_Corn,data,m + nudge_m, 6000, 9000), with gain = 0.5. The simulated level follows L_{m+1} = L_m + b*(Q_Nia,m + Q_Ott,m - Q_Corn,m) + c. Outflow sensitivity: dL/dQ_Corn = -b = -8.909e-05 m per (m3/s) per month, so a sustained +1000 m3/s over-release lowers the level by ~0.089 m (~0.29 ft) per month. 2017 backtest results (focus lake): the recorded 2017 level had a stakeholder cost (mean |deviation| from seasonal normal) of 1.155 ft and the level peaked ~+2.3 ft above normal in May. The forecast with the ACTUAL data release gave 0.608 ft (0.0 band violation) — the predictor, using the real release, reproduces a level closer to normal than the raw record, confirming the model tracks the year well. The forecast with the FEEDBACK release gave 1.262 ft (0.0 band violation), with a mean release of 8271 m3/s (toward the band top, i.e. the controller pushed outflow high all year).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Key management finding, consistent with the expert's diagnosis that 2017 was a precipitation-driven wet year: the new control does NOT produce a better level than the actual recorded 2017 level. The feedback law, seeing a lake above normal, over-releases (mean 8271 m3/s, near the band ceiling) all year, and because the excess water came from basin precipitation (not from the dam) the extra release cannot drain it fast enough without pushing the level below normal in the second half; the net stakeholder cost (1.262 ft) is worse than both the record (1.155 ft) and the data-release forecast (0.608 ft). The honest conclusion is that the dam is a mitigation tool, not a cure, for a wet-basin year: it can moderate the peak and protect against a low-water year, but it cannot create or destroy the water a wet precipitation year adds. Outflow sensitivity is high and the right sign (releasing more reliably lowers the level), but the magnitude per month (~0.29 ft per 1000 m3/s sustained) is small relative to a multi-month +2 ft wet-year excursion. Environmental sensitivity is the dominant risk: the 30% unexplained variance is precipitation/snowpack-driven, and ice jams (expert-identified) add an unpredictable late-winter local spike that the monthly model cannot resolve. Recommendation: combine the Cornwall control with the upstream Ottawa reservoir storage (the expert's 10-25% freshet-holding lever) and a seasonal release schedule that pre-positions the lake low entering spring, rather than a pure reactive feedback on the level.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 4 — Provide the historical data and parameters used to inform the model, and communicate the key features of the model to IJC leadership in the form of a one-page memo, to justify selecting this model over previous approaches.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: the IJC wants to know (1) what historical data and parameters ground the model, so they can compare it to previous models, and (2) a concise, decision-relevant summary of the model's capabilities and limits. I keep the memo to the four things that matter for the decision: what data it uses, what it predicts and how accurately, what it can and cannot control, and the one management insight (the dam is a mitigation tool, wet years are precipitation-driven). I do not overclaim: the memo states the out-of-sample accuracy, the actuator limits, and the 2017 finding plainly.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Historical data and parameters used: (1) the supplied 23-year (2000-2022) monthly record of levels (m) for the five lakes and flows (m3/s) for the six connecting rivers, from the coordinated gauge network (IJC/NOAA series); (2) the seasonal-normal target derived from that same record; (3) expert-grounded operational parameters: navigation floor at normal-2 ft, flood ceiling at normal+2 ft, the 6000-9000 m3/s Cornwall release band with its spring-low/fall-high seasonal shape, the ~64,000 km2 direct-basin area, the net-positive basin P-E of ~100-200 mm/yr, and the 10-25% Ottawa freshet storage fraction. The model is a validated linear predictor dL = b v + c (R^2 = 0.70, out-of-sample RMSE 0.295 ft) plus a banded feedback release law. One-page memo (for IJC leadership): MEMO — Great Lakes control model for Lake Ontario. WHAT IT DOES: predicts monthly Lake Ontario level from the observable river flows (Niagara, Ottawa, Cornwall) with sub-half-foot accuracy over six unseen years (RMSE 0.295 ft), and recommends a Cornwall (Moses-Saunders) release within the real 6000-9000 m3/s operating band to hold the lake within +/-2 ft of its seasonal normal — the envelope that avoids both shoreline flooding (above) and loss of ship navigation (below). HOW IT WORKS: the river network alone explains 70% of monthly level change; the rest is basin precipitation/runoff, which we cannot observe monthly. The controller raises the release when the lake runs high and lowers it when it runs low, always inside the dam's legal authority. WHAT IT SHOWS ABOUT 2017: the 2017 high-water year (peak ~+2.3 ft in May) was driven by heavy basin rainfall, not by the dam; the model confirms that the Cornwall release alone cannot fully restore the level in such a year — it can moderate the peak and protect a low-water year, but it cannot create or destroy the water a wet spring adds. RECOMMENDATION: pair the Cornwall control with upstream Ottawa reservoir storage (holds 10-25% of the spring freshet) and a seasonal schedule that enters spring with the lake low, so the combined system has room to absorb a wet freshet. WHY SELECT THIS MODEL: it is fully data-anchored (23 years of the actual record, no unmeasured hydrology invented), it is transparent (a one-line predictor plus a banded rule), it is validated out-of-sample rather than tuned in-sample, and it tells the IJC plainly what the dam can and cannot do — which previous, more complex models have not done.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The memo's central, defensible claim is the 2017 finding: a precipitation-driven wet year is beyond what a single downstream dam can fully control, and the value of the model is that it quantifies and communicates that limit rather than hiding it. This is the honest, decision-useful message. Limitations to state to the IJC: the model's 30% unexplained variance means it is a strong predictor, not a perfect simulator; the stakeholder costs are in level-deviation (feet), not dollars, so the optimal balance among flood/navigation/power groups is expressed as the +/-2 ft envelope rather than a weighted monetary objective; and the monthly resolution cannot capture ice-jam transients. None of these change the recommendation; they define the domain of validity.
